name: diffeq

members.name: odeint
members.signature: odeint(func: Callable[[Tensor, Tensor], Tensor], y0: Tensor, t: Tensor | Sequence[float], method: str | ButcherTableau = 'rk4', return_trajectory: bool = True)
members.summary: Integrate `dy/dt = f(t, y)` on a fixed grid with an explicit RK method.
members.extended:
The supplied grid `t` *is* the integration grid: consecutive entries are
stepped in one Runge-Kutta step each, with no sub-stepping and no dense
output.  Step size therefore comes from the spacing of `t`, and
controlling accuracy means choosing a finer grid.

Gradient mode is left entirely to the caller.  Under grad, the whole solve
is differentiable end-to-end (discretise-then-optimise) and every stage is
retained for backward; wrap the call in `lucid.no_grad` for sampling,
where the stage graph is pure overhead.

parameters.name: func
parameters.description:
Right-hand side `f(t, y) -> dy/dt`.  Receives the stage time as a
0-D tensor matching `y0` in dtype and device, and must return a
tensor with the same shape as `y0`.

parameters.name: y0
parameters.description: Initial state at `t[0]`.  Any shape; must have a floating dtype.

parameters.name: t
parameters.description:
Strictly monotonic 1-D grid of at least two finite time points.
Descending grids integrate backwards in time.

parameters.name: return_trajectory
parameters.description:
Return the state at every grid point.  Set `False` to keep only the
final state — for a sampling run of many steps over a batch of
images, stacking the full trajectory multiplies peak memory by the
number of steps.

returns.description:
Shape `(len(t), *y0.shape)` when `return_trajectory` is `True`
(index 0 is `y0` itself), otherwise `y0.shape`.  The dtype is the
promotion of `y0` with everything `func` returns, matching what
`y + dt * k` would produce.

raises.description:
If `t` is not a strictly monotonic 1-D grid of at least two finite
points, if `y0` has a non-floating dtype, if `method` names no
registered method, or if `func` returns a tensor whose shape or
device differs from `y0`.

If `method` is neither a string nor a `ButcherTableau`, or
if `func` returns something other than a tensor.

examples:
Exponential decay against its closed form:
>>> import lucid, lucid.diffeq as diffeq
>>> y0 = lucid.tensor([1.0])
>>> t = [i / 20 for i in range(21)]
>>> y = diffeq.odeint(lambda s, y: -y, y0, t, return_trajectory=False)
>>> abs(float(y.item()) - 0.36787944) < 1e-6
True
notes:
Cost is `(len(t) - 1) * method.stages` calls to `func`.  Adaptive step
control, error estimates, and the O(1)-memory adjoint are deliberately out
of scope here — they need a per-step error norm read back to the host,
which changes the performance character of the loop.

Higher-order differentiation works: the fused step opts into
graph-recording backward, so `create_graph=True` through a solve behaves
exactly as it would for the unfused arithmetic.

members.name: ButcherTableau
members.signature: ButcherTableau(a: tuple[tuple[float, ...], ...], b: tuple[float, ...], c: tuple[float, ...], order: int, name: str)

methods.name: stages
methods.summary: int: Number of stage derivatives evaluated per step.
methods.extended:
Equals the number of right-hand-side calls the method makes for each
step, which is the dominant cost when the right-hand side is a neural
network.

methods.name: __init__
methods.signature: __init__(a: tuple[tuple[float, ...], ...], b: tuple[float, ...], c: tuple[float, ...], order: int, name: str)

members.summary: Coefficient table defining one explicit Runge-Kutta method.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description:
Strictly lower-triangular stage coefficients, stored row by row with
the zeros above the diagonal omitted — row `i` holds exactly `i`
entries, so `a[0]` is empty.  Sequences of any kind are accepted
and coerced to nested tuples.

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Combination weights, one per stage.  Must sum to `1`.

parameters.name: c
parameters.description:
Stage times as fractions of the step.  Entry `i` must equal
`sum(a[i])`, the standard consistency condition.

parameters.name: order
parameters.description:
Order of accuracy $p$: halving the step size shrinks the global
error by roughly $2^p$.  Used by tests and diagnostics, never by
the integration loop itself.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Human-readable method name, surfaced in error messages.

raises.description:
If `a` / `b` / `c` disagree on stage count, if any row of `a`
has the wrong length for a strictly lower-triangular matrix, if `b`
does not sum to `1`, if any `c[i] != sum(a[i])`, or if `order`
or `name` are unset.

examples:
The classical fourth-order method, written out in full:
>>> import lucid.diffeq as diffeq
>>> rk4 = diffeq.ButcherTableau(
...     a=((), (0.5,), (0.0, 0.5), (0.0, 0.0, 1.0)),
...     b=(1 / 6, 1 / 3, 1 / 3, 1 / 6),
...     c=(0.0, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0),
...     order=4,
...     name="rk4",
... )
>>> rk4.stages
4

see_also.name: lucid.diffeq.odeint
see_also.description: Consumes a tableau, by name or by instance.

extended:
Numerical integration of ordinary differential equations, `dy/dt = f(t, y)`,
where the right-hand side is an arbitrary Lucid callable — most often a neural
network, as in continuous normalising flows, flow matching, and rectified flow.

Surface: `odeint` integrates on a fixed user-supplied grid using an
explicit Runge-Kutta method, and `ButcherTableau` is the coefficient
table it dispatches on.  The five built-in tableaux — `EULER`,
`MIDPOINT`, `HEUN2`, `HEUN3`, `RK4` — are also
exported, and a custom tableau is accepted anywhere a method name is.

Everything here is reached as `lucid.diffeq.*` and nowhere else — there are
no top-level aliases and no `Tensor` methods, so each name has exactly one
canonical path.

Adaptive step control, the O(1)-memory adjoint, and stochastic differential
equations are not implemented; the fixed-step explicit family is what the flow
model families need, and the rest have materially different performance
characteristics.

attributes.name: EULER
attributes.description: Forward Euler — one stage, first order.  Method name `"euler"`.

attributes.name: MIDPOINT
attributes.description: Explicit midpoint — two stages, second order.  Method name `"midpoint"`.

attributes.name: HEUN2
attributes.description:
Heun's method (explicit trapezoid) — two stages, second order.  Method
name `"heun2"`.

attributes.name: HEUN3
attributes.description:
Heun's third-order method — three stages, third order.  Method name
`"heun3"`.

attributes.name: RK4
attributes.description:
The classical Runge-Kutta method — four stages, fourth order.  Method
name `"rk4"`.
